title: Email Etiquette
intro: The right opening and closing for the right relationship — a friend, a boss, a stranger. Get it wrong and the whole email reads off.

A2.right: a stranger — very formal, name unknown
a close friend — very casual opening
family or close friend — affectionate closing
a colleague — friendly but professional closing
a named stranger or new contact — formal opening
a boss or client — polite professional closing

B1.right: a company you're applying to — formal, name unknown
colleagues you know well — friendly, semi-formal opening
a friend or familiar colleague — warm casual opening
a named formal contact — professional closing
a friendly colleague — casual British closing
an unknown recipient at an organisation — very formal opening
a friend — casual closing before a call or meeting
a client you know well — friendly professional closing

B2.right: a university tutor — formal opening with title
a very close friend — extremely casual opening

B2.left: I hope this message finds you well.
B2.right: a professional contact — formal, slightly old-fashioned opening
a friend or supportive colleague — warm casual closing
an unnamed formal recipient — closing when you don't know their name
a semi-formal contact — friendly, safe closing
a colleague you know — casual professional opening
a colleague or client — brief, appreciative closing

C1.left: I am writing on behalf of the board.
C1.right: a formal representative context — professional, authoritative opening
an old friend reconnecting — warm, enthusiastic opening
a formal complaint or error context — professional, remorseful
a very formal professional contact — polished, slightly old-fashioned closing

C1.left: Do give my regards to the family.
C1.right: a family friend — warm, polite closing

C1.left: I look forward to your prompt response.
C1.right: a formal business contact — professional closing with urgency
a close friend — casual, informal closing
a senior formal contact — deferential professional closing
